newsitem.title: USA: U.S. students know science facts, weak on analysis.
newsitem.headline: U.S. students know science facts, weak on analysis.

text.p: American students are learning the facts of science but are weaker in their ability to reason, experiment or analyse on their own, according to a new assessment of science education released Friday.

The test data, part of the federal National Assessment of Educational Programmes, is a snapshot of science education at grades 4, 8, and 12. The test is new and designed to set a benchmark for the future, not to compare today's performance to the past or to other countries.

"By the end of high school, most students seem to have some grasp of basic scientific facts and principles," said University of Michigan education expert Michael Nettles, a member of the National Assessment Governing Board.

Students can read graphs, and follow directions to carry out simple experiments. But when asked to go beyond that "to apply scientific knowledge to a new situation, to design an experiment themselves or to explain their reasoning clearly, the results are disappointing," Nettles told a conference in Washington where the results were released.

"We expect and hope that this test will notch up what our young people know about science as we move toward and into the 21st century," Secretary of Education Richard Riley said. "America has the best science in the world. Yet, the lack of knowledge about science among some Americans can be troubling."
Riley said this test was designed to spur more "hands on" science learning and teaching. But he noted that the country has learned "how to do a better job teaching science."

More students are taking advanced science courses, and science achievement tests have quantified progress. In addition, girls are closing the science gender gap with their male peers, although the gap is still significant among the highest achieving 12th graders, the ones most likely to go on to college and careers in science and technology.
The National Assessment of Educational Progress science assessment involved students in three grades doing earth, life, and physical science.
The tests involved some multiple choice answers but unlike many such assessments in the past it also required short essays and at least one hands-on experiment.
The national assessment programme dates back 25 years but has had a higher profile in recent years as part of the recent debate over national standards and voluntary national testing.
